passage:
Hi Mukund,
Work's good, mostly. The team hired Chandrika two weeks ago and honestly I knew in her first meeting she wasn't sharp. She took ten seconds to answer a simple question. Since then it's been one thing after another: she spelt the client's name wrong in an email, and she asked where the printer was, twice. I've started keeping a note of it. Our manager keeps praising her client summary, but that was probably easy stuff. And yes, she stayed late to fix the dashboard bug, but anyone could have done that. I'll tell you more when we meet. I'm rarely wrong about people.
Sachin

qa.q: What did the manager keep praising?
qa.a: The manager kept praising Chandrika's client summary.

qa.q: Why does it feel sensible to Sachin to keep a note of Chandrika's slips?
qa.a: Sachin feels confident, even proud of reading people, after the slow first answer, so each slip seems like more proof and each success like an exception.

qa.q: What could Sachin try to check that first impression?
qa.a: Sachin could keep a second list of her good work, like the client summary and the dashboard fix, and read both lists together before judging. Asking the manager what they valued in the summary would also help.

qa.q: How might Chandrika experience working next to someone who has already decided she is weak?
qa.a: She may sense that her effort, like staying late on the bug, is never noticed, which could make her anxious and less willing to ask simple questions.

grounding: Shows a young professional who judged a new colleague weak in her first meeting reading each small slip as proof while waving away her good work.

passage: You know, Varun, I'm the person on our team who spots weak links early. Pema's radar, everyone calls it. That new analyst, Hafsa? I had her figured out on day one. She asked what "the Q3 file" meant. Who asks that? Since then I notice everything: she sends reports at 6:02 instead of 6, she said sorry in one meeting three times. My lead says her data cleanup saved us a week. Fine, one good thing. But yesterday she missed a comma in a formula. See? That's the real Hafsa. People keep telling me to give her time. Why would I? I already know how this story ends.

qa.q: What does the lead say Hafsa's data cleanup did?
qa.a: The lead says her data cleanup saved the team a week.

qa.q: Why does Pema feel so sure about Hafsa after day one?
qa.a: Pema takes pride in spotting weak links early, so the first impression feels like skill rather than guesswork. Each small slip seems to confirm it, and the week saved gets filed as one good thing.

qa.q: What small step would help Pema judge Hafsa more fairly?
qa.a: Pema could list what Hafsa has actually delivered each week, including the cleanup, and ask whether a stranger reading that list would call her weak.

qa.q: How might Varun hear this story?
qa.a: Varun may notice that the evidence against Hafsa is tiny, like a comma and a two-minute delay, while the big result is waved away, and wonder how fair Pema is being.

grounding: Shows a young professional whose day-one impression of a new colleague turns each small slip into proof while her real results are dismissed.

passage: I sit between Arnab and the new designer, Meenal, so I've seen the whole thing. I'm Kalyani, by the way. On Meenal's first day she mixed up two client logos in a draft, and Arnab rolled his eyes and said, "Here we go." Since then he mentions every small thing in the morning meeting: a late reply, a font slightly off. Last Friday her poster for the festival campaign got the client's only compliment of the month. Arnab said the client was just being polite. I can't see inside his head; maybe he's stressed about his own work. But I notice he never says "good job" to her, and she's stopped showing him her drafts.

qa.q: What happened to Meenal's poster for the festival campaign?
qa.a: It got the client's only compliment of the month.

qa.q: What might Arnab be thinking when he calls the client's compliment just polite?
qa.a: He may feel irritated by Meenal and doubtful that anything good she does is real, because his day-one impression still feels true to him. Kalyani admits not knowing what is really in his head and wonders if he is stressed.

qa.q: How could Kalyani help without accusing Arnab?
qa.a: Kalyani could mention the compliment in the morning meeting alongside the small slips, or ask Arnab privately what Meenal would need to do to change his view.

qa.q: What is it like for Meenal to work next to Arnab?
qa.a: Meenal seems discouraged; she has stopped showing him drafts, which suggests she expects criticism whatever she does.

grounding: Shows a young professional who decided on day one that a new colleague was weak, now reading each slip as proof and dismissing her praised work.

passage:
Week one. At the Jaipur hotel's front desk, Jagdish, the shift supervisor, watched the new trainee, Afreen, freeze for a moment when a guest asked about the airport shuttle. He made a note in his head: slow. When she printed the wrong invoice that afternoon, he thought, there it is.
Week three. A family from Lyon praised Afreen by name in the feedback book for sorting out their lost luggage. Jagdish skimmed it and turned the page. That same evening she mistyped a room number, and he told the manager, "I did say she might not be right for the desk."
Week five. Preparing her review, Jagdish pulled up the logs to prove his point. Her check-ins were the fastest on the shift. He stared at the screen for a long moment, then deleted the first line he had written.

qa.q: What did the family from Lyon praise Afreen for?
qa.a: For sorting out their lost luggage.

qa.q: Why did Jagdish think "there it is" when Afreen printed the wrong invoice?
qa.a: Jagdish felt a satisfied certainty, because he had already decided on day one that she was slow, so the slip seemed to prove him right.

qa.q: In week five, what did Jagdish do that changed the review?
qa.a: He looked at the actual check-in logs, which showed Afreen was the fastest on the shift, and deleted the unfair first line. Checking the record instead of his memory was the turning point.

qa.q: How might Afreen have felt working under Jagdish in the first weeks?
qa.a: She may have sensed his doubt and felt nervous or watched, even while doing good work that seemed to go unnoticed.

grounding: A supervisor who judged a new trainee as weak on day one reads her slips as proof and skims her praise, until the logs show otherwise.

passage: Santosh, you're new to reviewing people, so let me confess something. In 1999 I was a young man of twenty-five, a sub-editor at a Lucknow newspaper, and they put a new reporter, Kamini, on my desk. On her first day she spelt a minister's title wrong. That was it for me. I'm Lalit, and I decided she was careless. After that, every comma she missed went into my little notebook. Her scoop on the flooded school? I told myself someone had tipped her off. Her clean copy on budget day? Luck. At the six-month review I read out my notebook. The editor listened, then pulled out a folder of her bylines and asked, "And these?" I had no answer. I'd been collecting only one kind of fact. So before you write anyone's review, look for what you've been skipping.

qa.q: What mistake did Kamini make on her first day?
qa.a: She spelt a minister's title wrong.

qa.q: Why did young Lalit put every missed comma into his notebook?
qa.a: Having decided early that Kamini was careless, he felt annoyed by each slip and saw himself as simply thorough. Good work didn't fit, so he explained it away as luck or a tip-off.

qa.q: What was the turning point for Lalit at the six-month review?
qa.a: The editor pulled out Kamini's bylines and asked "And these?", showing him the evidence he had been skipping.

qa.q: How might Kamini have felt if she had known about the notebook?
qa.a: She would likely have felt judged unfairly and discouraged, since her scoop and clean copy were being dismissed.

grounding: An older editor tells a new reviewer how he once judged a new reporter careless and noted only her slips, ignoring her good work.

passage:
"She sent the client file with the old logo again," Rehana said, dropping into the chair beside Faisal. "Told you on day one. Maria's not up to it."
"Again? That's the first time I've heard of it."
"Well, and last week she asked where the templates were."
"Everyone asks that. I asked that."
"And she took forty minutes for a ten-minute task."
Faisal frowned. "The audit summary? The client wrote back saying it was the clearest one they'd had."
"Luck. Or someone helped her."
"Rehana, who helped her?"
Rehana opened her mouth, then shut it. "I don't know. I just had a feeling about her from the interview. She seemed nervous."
"So you decided in the interview."
"I didn't decide anything." She stared at the logo on her screen. "Did I?"

qa.a: The client wrote back saying it was the clearest one they'd had.

qa.q: Why does Rehana feel her view of Maria is fair?
qa.a: Rehana feels sure and a little irritated, because each small slip seems to confirm the feeling from the interview, so it looks like evidence rather than a first impression.

qa.q: What could Rehana try before judging Maria again?
qa.a: She could write down Maria's good work, like the audit summary, next to the slips, and compare the slips with what other new staff usually do.

qa.q: How might Maria be affected if Rehana's view goes unchecked?
qa.a: Maria could be judged harshly for normal new-starter mistakes, and her strong work might never be credited.

grounding: A young professional reads a new colleague's small slips as proof she is weak and explains away her praised work.

passage: When Deepika joined our design studio in June, she mixed up two clients' colour files in her first week. I decided right then that she was careless. After that I saw it everywhere. A typo in her email? Careless. Five minutes late to stand-up? Careless. When our manager praised her packaging mock-up, I thought, fine, but she probably copied the reference. Then in October our manager said, "Avni, you sit next to her, you do her three-month review," and I had to list examples. My weak column had four small things. Her strong column, when I forced myself to be honest, had eleven, including the redesign that won us the bakery account. I sat there with my coffee going cold, feeling a bit sick. I'd been grading her against a story I wrote in June.

qa.q: How many items were in Deepika's strong column?
qa.a: Eleven, including the redesign that won the bakery account.

qa.q: Why did Avni feel sick while writing the review?
qa.a: Avni felt guilty and uncomfortable on seeing that the careless label from June had been steering every judgment while Deepika's good work was ignored.

qa.q: What habit could help Avni judge new colleagues more fairly?
qa.a: Keep a running list of both strengths and slips from the start, and ask whether the same slip from someone else would even be noticed.

qa.q: How might Deepika feel if she learned about the June label?
qa.a: Deepika might feel hurt and unfairly treated, since one early mix-up coloured how all her later work was seen.

grounding: A young designer looks back on reading every small slip by a new colleague as proof of carelessness while overlooking her strong work.

passage:
Supervisor's note, Pune service desk, 14 March
In today's review Omkar again rated Deepika "below expectations." His examples: one mistyped ticket number in her first week, a late log entry, and a question he called "basic." I checked the system. In the same six weeks she closed the most customer tickets on the team and got two thank-you emails, which Omkar had been copied on. When I showed him the numbers he said, "Maybe, but you can tell she's shaky." He looked genuinely surprised when I asked what she had done since week one that was shaky. He couldn't name anything recent. I've asked him to redo the review using only the ticket log, and I will sit with both of them on Friday.

qa.q: How many thank-you emails did Deepika get in six weeks?
qa.a: She got two thank-you emails, which Omkar had been copied on.

qa.q: Why did Omkar look surprised when asked for recent examples?
qa.a: He felt confident in his view, so it surprised and unsettled him to find it rested on week-one slips, not on anything recent.

qa.q: Why is redoing the review from the ticket log a good step?
qa.a: It makes Omkar work from the whole record instead of a first impression, so Deepika's closed tickets and thank-you emails count.

qa.q: How might Deepika be affected by the Friday meeting?
qa.a: She may feel relieved and fairly seen if her record is finally counted, though it may also hurt to learn how she was rated.

grounding: A supervisor records a young team member rating a new colleague as weak from first-week slips while ignoring her strong ticket record.

passage:
Thursday

New colleague Chandrika started on Monday. First day she was ten minutes late. I knew right then: not serious.

Tuesday she asked where the printer was. Obviously didn't read the onboarding doc. Wednesday she sent an email to the wrong client list, only two people, but still.

Today in the team meeting, Sir praised the pricing model she built. Honestly, I think someone helped her. Or it was a template.

I told Arun at lunch that she's weak and he'll see. He said her pricing model was actually clever. I said one good thing doesn't cancel three mistakes.

Walking home, I tried to remember something bad she did today. Couldn't. Still, I know my type.

— Leela

qa.a: Leela felt certain from the first late arrival, so each slip felt like proof and the good pricing model felt suspicious, which makes the judgement feel reasonable.

qa.q: What could Leela do to check the first impression?
qa.a: Leela could list everything Chandrika did this week, good and bad, and ask whether the late arrival would matter if the pricing model came first.

qa.q: How might Chandrika feel if she sensed Leela's judgement?
qa.a: Chandrika might feel unwelcome and anxious in her first week, not knowing why.

passage: At the small cooperative bank branch in Kalimpong, the new clerk, Maria, arrived in the cold December rain with a dripping umbrella and tracked mud across the floor. Tenzin, the assistant manager, sighed. Careless. After that he noticed everything. Maria stamped a form on the wrong page. Careless. She asked a customer to repeat his account number. Slow. When she stayed late to reconcile the cash register perfectly, Tenzin assumed the senior clerk had done most of it. When an elderly farmer came in specially to thank Maria for explaining his loan papers in Nepali, Tenzin was at lunch and heard about it later. "She's nice to old people," he said. "Doesn't make her good at the job." In the quarterly review, he rated her 'needs improvement.' The senior clerk read it and frowned.

qa.q: What did the elderly farmer thank Maria for?
qa.a: Explaining his loan papers in Nepali.

qa.q: Why did each small slip feel like proof to Tenzin?

qa.q: What could Tenzin do before the next review?
qa.a: He could note Maria's work every day for a month, including the cash reconciliation and the farmer's thanks, and ask the senior clerk for input.

passage:
On Nour's first week at the architecture firm in Amman, she spelled a client's name wrong in an email. Omar, who'd been there two years, noticed. Weak, he thought.

After that, he kept noticing. She arrived four minutes late on Tuesday. She asked where the printer paper was. She paused before answering a question in the review. Each one landed in the same mental file.

What didn't land: that her site drawings were cleaner than his. That the senior partner used her staircase sketch in the final pitch. That she'd stayed back to help the intern with a model. Omar saw all of it, and somehow it slid off.

At the monthly review, the partner asked for opinions on the new hires. Omar opened his mouth to say "not really up to it", and then saw Nour's staircase pinned on the wall behind the partner's head.

He paused. He couldn't remember a single real mistake since that email.

qa.q: What did Nour spell wrong in her first week?
qa.a: Nour spelled a client's name wrong in an email.

qa.q: Why did Omar's first impression feel so reliable to him?
qa.a: Omar felt certain after the email mistake, and each small slip seemed to confirm it, which made him feel observant rather than biased.

qa.q: What could Omar do before giving his opinion at reviews?
qa.a: Omar could list concrete work from the whole period, good and bad, like the staircase sketch and site drawings, before judging.

qa.q: How might Nour experience working with Omar if he never noticed his bias?
qa.a: Nour might feel quietly judged and unsupported despite doing strong work, and could lose confidence or be unfairly passed over.

grounding: A young professional decides early that a new colleague is weak and reads small slips as proof while ignoring her good work.

passage:
The pathology lab at the district hospital was busy on Monday morning when Zainab, the senior technician at twenty-five, got her new colleague: Vidya, fresh from training.

On day one Vidya labelled a sample tube in the wrong colour. Zainab corrected it and thought, careless.

For the next three weeks, Zainab kept a mental list. Vidya asked a question about the centrifuge. Vidya took a long lunch once. Vidya forgot to restock gloves.

She didn't keep a list of the other things. Vidya caught a mislabelled sample from another ward before it went out. Vidya calmed a frightened child for a blood draw in two minutes when nobody else could.

It was the head of department who pointed it out. "The ward sister says Vidya's the best with kids we've had," he said. "Agree?"

Zainab opened her mouth to say "she's careless", and realised she couldn't name one careless thing since day one that mattered.

qa.q: What colour mistake did Vidya make on day one?
qa.a: Vidya labelled a sample tube in the wrong colour.

qa.q: Why did Zainab keep noticing only Vidya's small slips?
qa.a: Zainab had decided on day one that Vidya was careless, so small slips felt like confirming evidence, and noticing them felt responsible.

qa.q: How could Zainab check her judgment of new staff in future?
qa.a: Zainab could note both slips and strengths each week, and ask others who work with the person before forming a view.

qa.q: How might Vidya feel if she sensed Zainab's view of her?
qa.a: Vidya might feel anxious and unfairly judged, working hard while her senior sees only small mistakes.

grounding: A young technician decides early that a new colleague is careless, collecting slips and missing her strong work.

Hi Ma'am,

You asked me to write down my view on Devika before her probation review. I've been honest in drafts, and I want to be honest about something else too.

In her first week, Devika misread a delivery date and I had to call the client to apologise. I decided then that she wasn't sharp. Since then, I've mentioned her small slips to you often: a late reply, a typo in a report.

But while writing this, I went through her work properly. She rebuilt the vendor sheet I'd been avoiding. She closed the Pune account I thought was lost. The client from week one now asks for her by name.

I think my first impression steered everything after it. I'd like to withdraw my earlier comments and recommend she be confirmed.

Sorry this is long.

Chaitanya

qa.a: Chaitanya felt uncomfortable and a little ashamed, realising the first impression had steered everything and the good work had been ignored.

qa.q: What countermeasure did Chaitanya use, and why did it help?
qa.a: Chaitanya reviewed all of Devika's actual work instead of relying on remembered slips, which showed evidence the first impression had hidden.

qa.q: How might Devika's probation have gone if Chaitanya had not written this?
qa.a: Devika might have been judged unfairly on a few small slips, despite rebuilding the vendor sheet and saving the Pune account.
